At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets).

Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded.

There is much to trouble teachers in Milburn’s review, but perhaps topping the list is that about 30% of Neets left school with good GCSEs or their equivalent. They did their part. They got the qualifications we drummed into them. But forgotten somewhere in the process was what we, as teachers, learned from countless interviews with prospective employers in our own youth: grades were never the full sum of our parts. Or to quote Milburn, young people must be provided with both the “aptitudes” as well as “qualifications”.

For those of us working in education, time has been one of our biggest impediments. With the GCSE curriculum being so content-heavy, anything not on the specification becomes sidelined. In practice, schools have tended to leave careers advice to a 30-minute meeting at the beginning of Year 11. Once a fixture of the Year 10, now less than half of GCSE pupils conduct work experience. This is why school leaders will no doubt welcome the report’s recommendation that at key stage 3, Years 7-9, schools should be given the power to use 10% of curriculum time as they see fit. Work experience must take up some of this freed time.

Schools should start by rethinking where to concentrate careers guidance and accept that leaving it to Years 10 and 11 is too late. At my local secondary school, a “careers carousel” is hosted each year for Year 8 pupils. Run like a freshers’ fair, pupils move from stall to stall, talking to professionals from the construction and carpentry industries, as well as office workers and nurses. It means that when GCSE options are chosen in Year 9, some pupils have a better understanding of how their choices might lead to the career goals they are beginning to set themselves.

Schools will also have to rethink how they share Year 9 subject choices with pupils. Too often, subjects can appear to have little to do with the world beyond the school gates. A Year 9 student deciding whether to choose a GCSE in food preparation and nutrition cannot always clearly see how that qualification can form the basis for an apprenticeship, degree apprenticeship or other meaningful work.

There will always be pupils who drift into listlessness because they draw a blank whenever their thoughts land on life after GCSEs. That blank is frightening and the young people who feel that fear rarely have the language to articulate it. They need an adult to ask what they would like to do when they grow up and the space to answer with a truthful shrug that they haven’t the faintest idea.

Milburn’s report recommends a “risk of Neet indicators” should be made mandatory for schools to use, or that a new test should be made statutory at key stage 3 to “identify pupils who need additional support”. Teachers might pause at this, because we already know which of our students are at risk of becoming Neet. They are pupils with special educational needs, those who will struggle to achieve grade 4 in all but a few of their GCSEs and those who, because of behaviour and poor attendance, already suspect they will “fail” and so reject the schools they believe have given them nothing. By Year 11, these are the students on reduced timetables, if they are still attending school at all. Their sense that they will be labelled disappointments is palpable in their rejection of the very corridors they feel have cemented that failure. For at-risk pupils, transition planning that starts years before a mad scramble at the end of Year 11 will only be effective if there are dedicated staff with the time to write and see the plan through.

If reached out to by Year 9, good careers advice could have those at risk open up about what interests them and the non-academic strengths that they do have. Are they great bakers? Do they have a knack for putting people at ease? Are they great with animals? Do they know an infinite amount about crochet patterns? Can they dissect the workings of an Audi Q7? Their interests and expertise are as ripe for career development as the grades they are awarded. Someone just needs the time to show them. For this to work however, schools need fully funded specialist careers leads.

On ambition, Milburn’s report cannot be faulted. Most of its recommendations meet the scale of the challenge before us. But any teacher reading it will want to know: where is the money? Until schools are given a definitive answer, we might find the most disadvantaged young people are yet again being promised futures no one has shown them how to reach.

title: Students face being 'turned away from college' over budget gap
summary: Elin Jones said the funding was a result of the "financial reality" the Welsh government are facing.
full_text:
Hundreds of students could be "turned away from college" if changes are not made to the Welsh government's draft budget, according to further education leaders.

They warn it will lead to a "dire situation" after a major UK-wide report highlighted the problem of young people not in education employment or training (NEET).

Finance Minister Elin Jones has set out spending plans for 2027-28 which included £851m for Medr settlement which would mean cuts to further education, College Wales said.

The Welsh government said it wanted to see increased opportunities for young people and was working with Medr to deliver a tertiary education system focused on supporting learners and driving economic growth.

Medr is the organisation which funds post-16 education and training in Wales.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, David Hagendyk, chief executive of Colleges Wales, said further education colleges were already getting insufficient funding to cover all their learners, with demand for places on the up.

"In Wales we are, this year, funding 5,000 learners without any support at all from the Welsh government," he said.

"We'll be in a situation where we have thousands of learners who are unfunded next year [and] hundreds of learners who get turned away from college if we don't get that additional funding."

Colleges have previously warned they did not have enough funding to meet the demand for some courses, particularly entry level programmes in areas such as construction and health and social care.

Students at Cardiff and Vale College have said they have found it "difficult" to get a job and the threat of AI means there was uncertainty about future opportunities.

Daniel, 16, said it felt "way easier" to get into education than it is to get a job and he has struggled despite using online resources.

"I think it's quite a wide issue. If you are really dedicated to finding a job, you will be able to find one," he added.

Charli, 17, said her friends have had more opportunities in smaller communities like her home town of Merthyr Tydfil, and there was uncertainty about the "permanence" of jobs with the threat of AI.

"I know that in college - despite having career ideals - not many are confident that they will be able to achieve it the way things are," she added.

But other students were more confident with opportunities already lined up once they finish their college education.

Lucas, 17, said he felt "lucky" to have a job offer lined up and said "if you look hard enough there are loads of opportunities".

Freddie, 16, was on a course that guaranteed a job at the end of it.

"I think I am fine, but I'm not so sure about others though," he added.

On the same day the Welsh government published its draft budget, a major report on work and young people was unveiled in Westminster.

The recommendations in former Labour minister Alan Milburn's report included more job support for under-25s, a shake-up of the benefits system and a legal right for young people to a route into education, training or work.

Following the Milburn report, the UK government announced it would fully fund college places for everyone aged 16 to 18 in England for 2027/28.

"On the one hand we had the Milburn review which was a comprehensive package of long-term reforms and proposals.

"On the other hand you had a Welsh government that really didn't rise to the moment," Hagendyk said.

Speaking in the Senedd chamber on Tuesday, Jones acknowledged "pressure" on the Medr budget, which also funds universities, suggesting there would be discussions about support for "these important sectors".

The draft budget settlement for Medr in 2027-28 amounted to a 0.9% cut, when inflation was taken into account, with a cash cut pencilled in for 2028-29.

Universities Wales said institutions were facing "the most challenging financial circumstances in living memory" which meant difficult decisions have been made to cut costs.

Last week Aberystwyth University said it would be making further savings which would result in fewer staff.

The Welsh government said: "We will be investing £1bn in support of our tertiary education system in the next year further to the £1bn invested in the current financial year."

It added that Medr's budget had been protected.

"The financial position of the higher education sector is extremely challenging. Our review of higher education is considering how the sector is funded and organised to secure a sustainable and successful system into the future," it said.

title: OPINION: For a well-prepared workforce, schools must rethink the kinds of skills that will be useful in a changing economy
summary:

The post OPINION: For a well-prepared workforce, schools must rethink the kinds of skills that will be useful in a changing economy appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
For years, the debate about artificial intelligence and jobs has understandably focused on which workers machines will replace. People are worried about job security, and employers are seeking efficiencies.

Yet as AI-supported tasks and outputs become increasingly commonplace in virtually every workplace, the conversation is shifting. It’s becoming clear that the best way for today’s K-12 students to “AI-proof” themselves is to lean into the human skills that AI can’t replicate.

Hiring data backs this up. A recent report found that when employers add duties to the jobs most exposed to AI, those new responsibilities are more than twice as likely to call for human strengths like empathy, judgment and creativity.

The shift is sharpest at the entry level. The same report found that junior positions with the highest AI exposure are seven times more likely than the least exposed ones to require skills like leadership and strategic thinking, which employers have traditionally sought in more experienced workers.

The message is not that automation poses no risk, or that fears of job loss are unfounded. Rather, it is that the costs of neglecting skills such as communication and collaboration are harder to ignore and that failure to develop durable skills heightens the risk.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

For many students, connecting what they’re learning today to how they’ll use their knowledge and skills in the future can be daunting. After all, they’re often hoping to simply pass algebra.

But employers and hiring managers can act today by engaging with their local schools. By helping students understand the skills they will need to thrive, employers can set the tone for tomorrow’s job candidates.

To create a well-prepared workforce, we must rethink how we teach these human skills from the start. Employers have been signaling this need for years.

America Succeeds and Lightcast’s 2025 analysis of 76 million job postings found that 76 percent required at least one “durable skill” — an ability that stays useful no matter how technology or job titles change — and 8 of the 10 most-requested skills were durable.

These uniquely human skills matter more than most anything else on a resume. But schools rarely teach them explicitly.

Calling critical thinking, communication and collaboration “soft skills” understates their importance in school and the workplace.

Critical thinking helps students interpret complex experiments and workers identify convincing but incorrect AI-generated answers. Communication enables students to build evidence-based arguments and helps teams turn analysis into action. Collaboration prepares students for group projects and workplace disagreements that technology alone cannot resolve.

AI’s promise depends on these skills, too. In a recent global survey, workers who said they used AI to save time estimated that nearly 40 percent of those savings are lost to correcting, clarifying or rewriting low-quality AI-generated content. The company that commissioned the survey called this an “AI tax on productivity.”

The technology didn’t eliminate the necessary thinking. It just moved the burden downstream to a person who must catch the mistake.

The strongest preparation for work in an AI-empowered economy combines domain knowledge and AI fluency — and the human skills to apply both appropriately. And this preparation must begin well before a graduate’s first job.

Related: OPINION: Want to get young people excited about learning? Give them hands-on programs, mentors and skills that lead to good careers

To ensure that durable skills are treated as integral components of a student’s overall education, more than 20 states have adopted frameworks that emphasize communication, collaboration, critical thinking, resilience and other capabilities essential to work and civic life.

The challenge, as educators have readily found, is moving those commitments from strategic plans into students’ daily experiences. Insufficient shared conviction, structural constraints and a lack of coherence can hinder this work.

A district can embrace the ethos of durable skills initiatives — often called “portraits of a graduate” — while leaving the systems that shape classroom learning largely unchanged.

The teaching of durable skills should not be thought of as just another initiative competing for time with the teaching of reading, mathematics and science. Durable skills are the medium through which academic knowledge becomes understanding.

Educators looking to ensure that their students are well prepared for future careers don’t need to start new schools or redesign their entire curricula.

Instead, taking a few steps can help communities build on the systems they already have. Start by making sure students are developing durable skills within the curriculum. These skills should be explicitly taught, practiced and demonstrated alongside academic content. Choose instructional materials that help students build the competencies employers value.

Students must be taught how to explain their reasoning, evaluate competing evidence, revise their work after feedback and defend their decisions. Tasks that are part of the curriculum can make student progress on these capabilities visible without adding another layer of testing.

Finally, educators must learn to evaluate curated examples of student work, using clear criteria, with time to compare and calibrate evidence of learning. That will help teachers recognize what growth looks like across subjects and grade levels. It will also help students and families understand what an abstract phrase like “critical thinking” actually means.

These opportunities must reach every student, not only those in well-resourced schools or selective programs.

None of us can predict what tools today’s students will be using in their jobs 10 years from now. But we do know they’ll need to think clearly, speak up with confidence and work well with other people — no matter what’s on the screen in front of them.

AI didn’t create that truth. It just made it impossible to ignore.

Sari Factor is vice chair and chief strategy officer at Imagine Learning.

title: Can Colleges Help More Students Maintain Financial Aid Eligibility?
summary:
Can Colleges Help More Students Maintain Financial Aid Eligibility? kathryn.palmer… Wed, 11/18/2026 - 06:00 AM In 2025, approximately 960,000 students lost federal financial aid after failing a government-mandated academic progress check, a new report shows. Byline(s) Kathryn Palmer Can Colleges Help More Students Maintain Financial Aid Eligibility?
kathryn.palmer… Wed, 11/18/2026 - 06:00 AM

In 2025, approximately 960,000 students lost federal financial aid after failing a government-mandated academic progress check, a new report shows.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
About half of college students who fail to meet the government’s academic progress standards lose access to federal financial aid by the following semester. But some simple policy adjustments may help more maintain aid, argues a new report from the Lumina Foundation and Mathematica.

Federal law mandates that colleges and universities monitor whether students who receive federal grants and aid are making satisfactory academic progress (SAP)—measured by grades, pace and time to completion—as an accountability measure. However, failing SAP requirements isn’t always a reflection of a student’s inadequate effort or aptitude. Instead, it’s often the result of adverse circumstances, said Janai Raphael, strategy officer for access at the Lumina Foundation.

Take, for example, a mother of two who was doing well juggling childcare, work and college courses until her boss changed her schedule, Raphael said. She started missing classes, her grades slipped and by the end of the semester, she’d failed the SAP requirements and lost her financial aid.

“Now, to get back on track academically, she has to take more classes. But without financial aid, she’s going to have to pay for those classes out of pocket,” Raphael said at a media briefing about a report. “So what was initially a difficult semester has now become a substantial financial barrier that could keep her from continuing her education altogether.”

According to the report, 91.5 percent of institutions said students commonly say they struggle to meet SAP due to life circumstances affecting attendance. Another 85.3 percent cited health challenges, compared to 51.9 percent who cited insufficient academic preparation.

At the same time, a middle-aged returning college student whose transcript from 20 years ago doesn’t meet SAP requirements is also ineligible to receive federal aid and re-enroll.

Colleges are “actively encouraging these adults to come back, but we need to understand if our policies are actually making that return possible,” Raphael said. “Until recently, we just simply didn’t have a clear national picture about how many students are actually being impacted by SAP.”

Lost Opportunities

To fill that gap, researchers analyzed the SAP policies of 1,200 two- and four-year institutions, surveyed more than 200 financial aid offices, and interviewed numerous students, financial aid administrators and academic advising and financial aid support staff at more than 22 institutions.

According to the study, 1.8 million undergraduates failed to meet SAP requirements during end-of-term or end-of-year evaluations in spring 2025. The failure rate was higher at two-year institutions (22 percent) than at public (8 percent) or private four-year institutions (5 percent). And as a result, approximately 960,000 of those undergraduates lost their financial aid eligibility.

But colleges and universities have the power to help more students keep their financial aid, according to the report. It cites institutions’ poor communication about SAP requirements and a lack of interest in changing SAP implementation as explanations for why so many students lose their financial aid.

Although federal law allows institutions to adopt optional policies to make their SAP requirements more lenient, most haven’t done so.

According to the report, only about one-quarter of students attend institutions with a laddered GPA requirement, while two in three attend a college that counts remedial courses toward maximum time to degree completion. That “may make SAP harder, because students in developmental courses must attempt and pass more courses in total to complete their degree,” the report reads. In addition, “some institutions deliberately choose stricter SAP requirements to align with the institution’s higher overall academic standards or to encourage students who are unlikely to be successful in the short term to withdraw rather than incur further student loans.”

Ira Nichols-Barrer, principal researcher at Mathematica and co-author of the report, said there’s also “pressure [for financial aid offices] to herd together.” Despite the “opportunity to try alternative approaches to SAP that are allowed under current federal rules, there’s a lot of institutions that either don’t know about that or are too hesitant to try.”

And while any student who loses financial aid after failing SAP requirements can file an appeal, the report found that only about one-fourth do so. That’s another missed opportunity, Nichols-Barrer added, because most appeals succeed in preserving aid eligibility for at least one term—and often trigger academic recovery support systems.

“It’s not just that their aid is extended. Most institutions are actually helping students stay enrolled after they have an appeal approved,” he added. “There’s just a gap here in the students getting into that pipeline of additional supports.”

title: UNC Chapel Hill Fined $5M for Admitting Too Many Out-of-State Students
summary:
UNC Chapel Hill Fined $5M for Admitting Too Many Out-of-State Students jessica.blake@… Wed, 11/18/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Jessica Blake UNC Chapel Hill Fined $5M for Admitting Too Many Out-of-State Students
jessica.blake@… Wed, 11/18/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
For the second year in a row, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill has admitted more out-of-state students than allowed under state policy. As a result, the flagship must pay the UNC system a fine of roughly $5 million.

Out-of-state-students make up 20 percent of this year’s freshman class—two percentage points more than the state’s 18 percent limit, The News & Observer reported. Under current policy, Chapel Hill’s fee will be used to support need-based scholarship programs across the system.

The flagship’s vice chancellor for communications, Dean Stoyer, said that his institution accepts responsibility for violating the system policy and is “refining” its models to avoid encountering the same problem again.

“We use established enrollment models to estimate how many admitted students from North Carolina and out of state will choose Carolina,” Stoyer told The News & Observer in an emailed statement. “Those decisions vary from year to year, and even a small shift can affect both the size of the incoming class and how many students enroll from each group. Our goal is to fill the first-year seats we have available while staying within the cap. We are refining our models to better meet both goals.”

This is the second time in the last decade the Chapel Hill institution has been penalized for exceeding the out-of-state ratio. The university was charged $1 million in 2016. The fine, levied after a university violates the policy for two years running, is calculated by multiplying the number of students admitted over the cap by the cost of out-of-state tuition.

The News & Observer also reported that the UNC system is considering changing the policy so that institutions are fined any time they violate the ratio, not just after they violate it for two consecutive years. The policy change would also create more flexibility for what the fine dollars can fund. Under the proposal, the fee could support not only need-based aid but also enrollment initiatives and “other strategic initiatives determined by the president.”

The system’s Board of Governors is slated to vote on these policy amendments later this week.

title: Presidents Weigh In on Politics, Scandal and Sports
summary:
Presidents Weigh In on Politics, Scandal and Sports Josh Moody Wed, 11/18/2026 - 03:00 AM Despite a new Democratic majority in Congress, which is expected to restrain the Trump administration’s attacks on higher ed, college presidents are still treading carefully. Byline(s) Josh Moody Presidents Weigh In on Politics, Scandal and Sports
Josh Moody Wed, 11/18/2026 - 03:00 AM

Despite a new Democratic majority in Congress, which is expected to restrain the Trump administration’s attacks on higher ed, college presidents are still treading carefully.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
NEW YORK CITY—College presidents may have new allies on Capitol Hill, but old problems persist.

Seven university leaders grappled with pressing issues at a dinner with journalists Monday night in New York City, where topics included uncertainty over federal research funding, campus sexual assault, the escalating costs of college athletics and multiple other pressing issues.

A new host led the dinner—now in its 39th year—for the first time since 2002: University of Tennessee–Knoxville Chancellor Donde Plowman stepped in for Arizona State University President Michael Crow, who couldn’t make it to the event due to flight issues.

Inside Higher Ed was on hand to hear what the presidents had to say as they prepare for a new Congress while continuing to navigate the Trump administration’s policy agenda.

The Federal Policy Outlook

The sector has been rocked by whiplash over the last two years as colleges scramble to comply with—or legally challenge—new government rules around diversity, equity and inclusion programs; admissions; international enrollment; research funding; and more. While this month’s “blue tsunami” swept a strong Democratic majority into Congress—where they are expected to push back on much of the Trump administration’s education agenda—college presidents are still apprehensive about what lies ahead.

Asked about their priority issues when the new Congress gets underway, presidents pointed to the need to stabilize federal research funding and ease restrictions on international student enrollment. But the concerns they take to Congress may be determined as much by litigation as legislation, as court fights over everything from DEI-related funding freezes to the mandatory reporting of admissions data continue to play out.

Syracuse University Chancellor Michael Haynie noted that the new Congress will not likely disregard the public’s mounting discontent over the high cost and murky value of higher ed; though the newly elected Democrats did not articulate a clearly defined education policy agenda, many candidates expressed concern about student loan debt, college access and affordability. (Some Democrats also highlighted academic freedom and free speech concerns on the campaign trail.)

“I don’t think it should be assumed that because another party is taking control of [Congress] they’re going to be receptive to this idea that everything is fine in higher education,” Haynie said.

Other leaders said they aren’t planning to become more vocal about their policy concerns and priorities to the new Democratic Congress, but will continue to advocate for their institutions quietly behind closed doors.

Pennsylvania State University President Neeli Bendapudi noted that she and her peers will lean on groups such as the Association of American Universities, the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities, and the American Council on Education to take their message to Capitol Hill.

She argued, “It’s not what we say on the microphones or what we say in public, but the conversations that we all have all the time behind closed doors with our government relations folks, with our alumni, all speaking up together” that will ultimately have the greatest impact.

Handling Sexual Assault

The recent sexual assault uproar at Cornell University also hung over the dinner as reporters questioned what presidents should know about such incidents and whether they are re-evaluating the role of Greek life, given the many campus controversies that arise involve fraternities. Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff has admitted he did not follow up on the allegations of gang rape in 2024, or the aftermath for both the victim and the accused, sparking criticism of how he handled the incident and questions about what campus leaders should know and how they should react.

Multiple presidents in attendance noted that they receive reports on Title IX cases on their campus, and some said they are briefed on every investigation. But knowing is one thing; preventing and investigating sexual assault is more challenging, they said.

Fordham University President Tania Tetlow, a former prosecutor and longtime director of a domestic violence clinic, noted that while many universities are focused on sexual assault prevention, little federal research exists on the efficacy of such efforts.

“There’s not a lot of evidence that they work, and what research shows is the rates of sexual violence are just as high off of college campuses with this age group as they are on,” Tetlow said. “We are battling the evils of the world, and we are doing it without a lot of help.”

Plowman noted that as participation in Greek life has boomed at Tennessee, the university has responded by tripling the number of staff members overseeing fraternities and sororities. Still, she acknowledged the need for more work on bystander intervention, given the apparent failure by any members of Cornell’s now-banned Chi Phi fraternity to intervene in the alleged gang rape.

But despite the many headline-grabbing issues attached to Greek life—including hazing as well as sexual assault—presidents dismissed the idea of doing away with such campus organizations. Some noted that disbanding fraternities and sororities would push their activities underground, where universities would have less control over them. Others touted the service and philanthropic work such organizations do.

The Cost of Big-Time Athletics

College athletics was another topic that drew robust conversation and disagreement. Asked by Inside Higher Ed how colleges square athletics programs—which overwhelmingly lose money—with the mission of affordability, some presidents emphasized the role of sports as a marketing tool and noted the hundreds of scholarships provided to student athletes across a variety of programs.

University of Colorado Boulder Chancellor Justin Schwartz said football coach Deion Sanders, an NFL Hall of Famer, is better known than the scholars at his institution who have won Nobel prizes. And that visibility, he said, has driven applications to the university since Sanders was hired in late 2022.

“I worry about what the world will be like with athletics on its current trajectory. I also worry about what our world will be like without it because of that visibility and the impact that it has,” Schwartz said. “It’s difficult to just do a real bottom-line financial assessment, because I don’t know how much I’d have to spend in marketing if I didn’t have college sports.”

Plowman echoed his point, noting that 43 million viewers watched the Tennessee Volunteers compete in various sports last year, bringing more attention to the university.

But Tetlow took a more critical view, arguing that the use of funds “that should be going to education” but are diverted to athletics is not defensible and that such allocations (often funded by student fees) should be “a bigger part of the story of the affordability crisis in higher ed.” She noted that many universities that rely on sports “as part of their identity, as part of their survival mechanism” are caught up in an arms race that compels more athletic funding to compete.

“The game is increasingly rigged,” Tetlow said. “It’s harder and harder to have this make sense.”

Presidents also noted that colleges have failed to effectively govern athletics, prompting some leaders to push for Congress to intervene and establish guidelines in the constantly evolving world of college athletics. (The Protect College Sports Act, which would address such hotly debated issues as player eligibility, compensation and student transfers, among other things, appears to be stalled in the final weeks of the current Congress; many experts predict that the new Democratic majority is unlikely to revive the bill next year.)

Bendapudi—whose institution, Penn State, is one of the few universities in the nation with a self-sustaining athletics program—said that while she loves the “trite analogy” of athletics as the front porch of the university, institutions need to remain committed to their true purpose. Without education at their core, she said, “We’ll have an amazing porch and no house behind it.”

title: Stopped-out student population reaches 37.8M, data finds
summary: About 1.9 million people in this group left higher education recently, according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Some 37.8 million U.S. working-age adults left college before completing a credential as of the start of the 2024-25 academic year, according to new data released Thursday by the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center.

That’s an increase of 1.3%, or about 500,000 people, from the prior year. About 1.9 million stopped-out students left higher education recently, last enrolling in 2022, the clearinghouse said.

Researchers also found more than 1 million working-age students who had previously stopped returned to higher education in 2023-24, representing a reenrollment rate of 2.7%

Dive Insight:

The stopped-out population, which represents nearly 1 in 5 working-age adults nationwide, has become an increasingly important pool of potential recruits as the sector confronts shrinking numbers of traditional-age students.

The majority of stopped-out students who return to higher education select new institutions to attend. Just over a third of returning students in the 2024-25 academic year, 34.4%, reenrolled at a college they previously attended, according to researchers.

One type of higher ed institution is particularly well positioned to benefit from returning students.

In 2023-24, public two-year colleges were the most popular type of institution for reenrolling stopped-out students who did not return to their original college. For example, 45.4% of students who previously attended a public four-year college enrolled at a community college in 2023-24, while just 18% returned to their original institution type.

Over half of students returning to higher ed, 53.2%, pursued an associate degree.

Stopped-out students were more likely to return to higher ed and earn a credential if they had completed a significant amount of coursework prior to disenrolling, according to the clearinghouse.

Among those who completed at least two years of full-time enrollment, 7.5% returned to college in the following decade, compared to 2.7% of the overall stopped-out population. And 8.5% earned a credential within their first year back, compared to 4.7% more broadly.

title: Court blocks DHS policy limiting international student training opportunities
summary: The higher education groups suing to strike down new limits on the Curricular Practical Training program are likely to succeed, a federal judge ruled.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The Trump administration may not enforce two recent policy memos that put new limits on international students’ ability to participate in internships and other training opportunities, per a federal court order Tuesday.

For decades, the Curricular Practical Training program has allowed international students to participate in off-campus training opportunities that result in academic credit. But in August, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security issued two memos barring international students from participating in such training programs unless they were mandatory to complete their degrees.

U.S. District Judge Julia Kobick temporarily blocked DHS from enforcing the two memos, ruling that the higher education associations who are suing to strike down the policy were likely to succeed.

Dive Insight:

The lawsuit was brought by prominent higher education groups, including the Association of American Universities. They argued that DHS unlawfully changed decades of “settled agency interpretation” when it issued its new two memos.

DHS pushed back in court documents, arguing that the two memos didn’t alter “the legal regime” because they were simply reminders about the CPT program’s regulatory requirements. However, Kobick wrote that they “represent a marked departure” from the agency’s prior interpretation.

Since 1991, the federal government has allowed international students to qualify for training opportunities — even if they weren’t mandated by their degree program — so long as they resulted in academic credit, Kobick wrote.

Yet in the August memos, DHS put new restrictions on the CPT program without acknowledging that it was shifting long-standing federal policy. Under its interpretation, an international student could only participate in a training opportunity like an internship if it was required of all students in their degree program.

“In practice, for example, this meant that a law school could not authorize CPT for a law student on an F-1 visa to extern for a federal judge for academic credit unless such an externship was required of all students seeking to earn a juris doctor degree,” Kobick wrote.

DHS also threatened college officials with civil and criminal liability if they didn’t comply with the memos.

Many colleges responded to the two memos by rejecting or revoking CPT authorization for some of their international students or by adjusting their program requirements.

At Columbia University, in New York, officials denied CPT authorization to over 120 international students this fall, according to court documents. Similarly, over a dozen international students at Grinnell College, in Iowa, lost out on internships due to the change.

Some colleges — including Cornell and Michigan State universities — reported that they’ve lost international students due to the two directives. And college officials have reported reluctance to sign documents related to the program over fear of being prosecuted.

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which operates under DHS, said in an email Wednesday that it does not comment on pending litigation.

title: PASSHE moves to close Commonwealth University’s Mansfield campus
summary: The public college system’s leader said the campus faces persistent deficits and long-running enrollment declines.

Dive Brief:

The leader of Pennsylvania’s State System of Higher Education is calling for the closure of Commonwealth University’s Mansfield campus by summer 2028.

In a public letter Tuesday, PASSHE Chancellor Christopher Fiorentino directed Commonwealth President Jeffery Osgood to submit a plan for an “orderly wind-down” of the campus by Dec. 8.PASSHE’s board of governors must approve the wind-down.

The closure is necessary for the public university’s “long-term financial stability” and to reduce systemic risks to PASSHE, Fiorentino said. A PASSHE faculty union leader on Tuesday vowed to “take every step necessary to fight this terrible plan.”

Dive Insight:

The push to close Commonwealth’s Mansfield campus comes nearly two years after the university moved to eliminate its smallest campus in Clearfield, which is set to close after the current academic year.

Mansfield’s closure would leave Commonwealth with two campuses — its main location in Bloomsburg and one in Lock Haven. The university was created in 2022 out of the merger of Bloomsburg, Lock Haven and Mansfield universities.

By the numbers

$7,825

The financial loss per full-time equivalent student at the Mansfield campus in the 2025-26 academic year.

3 in 5

Student housing beds empty on the Mansfield campus at the start of the fall 2026 term, which contributed significantly to its budget deficit.

802

Projected Mansfield student count for fall 2028, which would represent a 77.5% collapse from 2009.

16.3%

Projected decline in high school graduates in Mansfield’s home county of Tioga between the 2027-28 and 2036-37 academic years.

In justifying his decision to shutter Mansfield, Fiorentino cited cratering headcounts as well as persistent financial losses and local demographic shifts. He presented these factors as a drag on the university and PASSHE as a whole.

Between 2009 and 2026, Commonwealth’s Mansfield campus fall headcount plummeted 71.6% to 1,013 students, according to PASSHE data.

That count is projected to drop by another 200-plus students by fall 2028 amid declining first-year student enrollment and second-year retention rates, according to data in Fiorentino’s letter. He also pointed to estimates of falling high school graduate numbers in the surrounding counties.

“Fewer new students are enrolling at the Mansfield campus, reducing tuition revenue and putting additional pressure on the university's finances,” the PASSHE chancellor wrote to Osgood.

Fiorentino pointed to state funding meant to help Mansfield, including $75 million in one-time money used in part to clear the campus’s debt. And still the campus’s unrestricted deficit grew to $7.7 million for fiscal 2026.

Closing the campus would “reduce the likelihood that Commonwealth University would need to draw upon the reserves held by the other PASSHE universities,” Fiorentino said.

But a faculty union blasted the plan. Kenneth Mash, president of the Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties, said in a statement Tuesday that closing Mansfield would “ravage public higher education in Pennsylvania, create additional higher-education deserts, and hurt students.”

“This news came as a surprise, and it is unfortunate that the System has decided to approach this plan clandestinely,” Mash said. “We will not let Pennsylvania give up on our commitment to provide the opportunity for our students to earn a high-quality, low-cost public higher education. We will fight for Mansfield.”

On a FAQ page, PASSHE said it anticipates layoffs at the Mansfield campus but that it will adhere to collective bargaining agreements and “work to minimize the impact on university employees.”

As part of the wind-down plan for Mansfield, Fiorentino directed Osgood to detail arrangements for the campus's current students to finish their degrees with Commonwealth.

Commonwealth as a whole faces a $17 million operating deficit and recently announced that it could slash 175 jobs to help close the budget gap.

title: ABA accreditation arm moves to nix full-time faculty standard for first-year classes
summary: The U.S. Department of Justice recently threatened an antitrust probe over the requirement, arguing that it drives up legal education costs.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The American Bar Association’s accreditation arm voted last week to nix a requirement that the law schools it oversees have full-time faculty teach “substantially all” of their first-year classes.

The ABA’s accreditation council has been considering the change for months. However, the vote came a month after the U.S. Department of Justice warned the council that it could face an antitrust investigation if it didn’t change the standard.

Before the change is finalized, the ABA’s House of Delegates will review the policy shift at its next meeting in February and provide feedback. Afterward, however, the accreditation council can make the final call on whether to implement the change.

Dive Insight:

The ABA’s accreditation council voted to eliminate the standard while under pressure from the Justice Department. In an October letter, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the group could face an antitrust investigation if it didn’t eliminate the full-time faculty requirement, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Woodward argued that adjunct faculty are less expensive to hire and often have more firsthand experience, and that limiting their role in first-year law school education drives up costs and hurts students, the Journal reported.

The accreditation council also plans to seek public comment on further potential changes to its policies regarding full-time instructors that are meant to provide more flexibility to law schools.

The council is in communication with the Justice Department, a spokesperson for the council said Tuesday. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

Woodward’s letter came after the ABA’s accreditation council began seeking public comment in September on proposed changes to its full-time faculty requirements.

The accreditation council’s proposals drew mixed reactions from law schools and professors.

In a public comment, the faculty leadership of the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school opposed nixing the requirement regarding the first year of curriculum.

They argued that the first-year of law school “is a key period for educating students on core legal principles, doctrines, and analytical methods” and “a critically important time for creating community among law school students.”

“Full-time faculty are simply more available for answering student questions outside of class, as it is part of their full-time job to do so,” the faculty leaders wrote. “And perhaps most importantly, full-time faculty build pedagogical expertise in designing courses, sequencing learning, assessing progress, and giving constructive feedback.”

Yet others voiced support for the change. Terence Lau, dean of Syracuse University’s law school, argued that the changes would reduce “undue burden” while still preserving full-time faculty members’ “core role” in legal education.

Lau argued the current standard limits the ability for law schools to tap sitting judges or emeritus professors for first-year instruction. “Law schools should be able to draw on these teachers where they best serve students,” he wrote.

Last week’s vote comes as the accreditation council is under the microscope by the Trump administration.

In August, a report from U.S. Department of Education staffers recommended that the agency strip the ABA’s accreditation council of federal recognition. The staffers concluded that the council wasn’t compliant with over two dozen federal criteria and alleged that it wasn’t sufficiently independent from the ABA’s professional organization.

Losing federal recognition would mean the ABA’s accreditation council could no longer serve as a gatekeeper to Title IV financial aid. Although the group accredits some 200 law schools, only five rely on it for access to federal aid, a council representative said in September to a federal advisory panel reviewing the department’s findings.

That panel, which advises the Education Department on accreditation matters, deadlocked on a vote on whether to recommend that the council lose recognition. Education Under Secretary Nicholas Kent is soon expected to make a final call on the matter.

title: Teacher prep programs probed in Education Department’s latest anti-DEI push
summary: The agency said diversification efforts disregard "merit," but critics say the programs level the playing field for historically excluded candidates.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

The U.S. Department of Education opened a string of investigations into teacher preparation programs on Nov. 13, alleging that they discriminate on the basis of race under Title VI or sex under Title IX.

The investigations mark one of the first times the department's Office for Civil Rights has used civil rights protections to challenge diversification efforts in teacher scholarships, hiring, training and recruitment practices.

The programs at the center of the investigations are aimed at recruiting historically underrepresented groups in the teaching profession, such as men and teachers of color.

Among those programs are:

The City of the University of New York's NYC Men Teach Program.

The University of Maryland School of Education and Maryland Higher Education Commission Teacher Quality and Diversity Grant Program.

The Minnesota Department of Education's Education Tuition Assistance Program.

Minnesota's Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship Pilot Program.

“Race, national origin, or sex should not decide who will shape America’s next generation, yet many states and universities seem to prioritize recruiting and training ‘minority’ candidates rather than evaluating candidates based solely on merit,” said Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey in a Nov. 13 statement.

“Education agencies and institutions that consider race, national origin, or sex as a means to withhold opportunities in selecting, supporting, and preparing teaching candidates violate federal law and compromise education excellence."

Richey concluded that students should be "judged on their hard work and merit, not prejudged by the color of their skin or their sex.”

Using civil rights enforcement to preserve inequities?

EdTrust, a nonprofit that advocates for racial and economic equity in American education, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that the Trump administration is using civil rights protections meant to "dismantle discrimination and expand opportunity" to instead "undermine pathways into teaching for people historically excluded from the profession betrays that purpose."

“The administration’s false divide between ‘merit’ and diversity perpetuates the damaging suggestion that teachers of color are less qualified or less deserving," said Eric Duncan, director of Pre-K-12 policy of EdTrust, in the Nov. 16 statement. "It discounts their skills, expertise, and contributions while ignoring the systemic barriers that have denied talented people opportunities for generations. Scholarships that address those barriers help ensure that family wealth does not determine who can become a teacher."

The Education Department's investigations, Duncan said, "risk turning civil rights enforcement into a tool for preserving the very inequities it should confront.”

CUNY, which houses the NYC Men Teach Program being investigated by the department, said in a statement to K-12 Dive that it was "proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin."

According to the city's website, the program was created around 2015 in collaboration with the federal Education Department and then-Mayor Bill de Blasio with the goal of putting an additional 1,000 men of color into the city’s teacher pipeline.

A March 2026 evaluation of the program conducted for the NYC mayor's office by Westat, which provides research services for government agencies, shows that the program contributed over 3,100 new male teachers of color to New York City Public Schools between school years 2015–16 and 2023–24.

The American Association of Colleges for Teacher Education said in a Nov. 16 email to K-12 Dive, “Strengthening and diversifying the educator pipeline is essential to addressing persistent teacher shortages and ensuring every PK-12 student has access to well-prepared, effective teachers. Decades of research confirm that a diverse educator workforce benefits all students academically, socially, and emotionally."

AACTE added that it does not comment on active federal inquiries involving specific institutions or state agencies.

Other Trump administration efforts affect teacher pipeline

While the investigations are some of the first of their kind by OCR, they build on previous efforts by the Trump administration to weed out DEI in teacher preparation programs — especially in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard.

Some of the earliest federal grants terminated in 2025 by the administration were under the Supporting Effective Educator Development Grant Program, the Teacher Quality Partnership Program and the Teacher and School Leader Incentive Program, due to what it said was the promotion of "divisive ideologies". The department admitted in a March court filing that it had cancelled 104 out of 109 active TQP and SEED grants.

The loss of over 100 federal teacher training grants last year caused at least 127 teacher candidates to drop out of their programs and another 259 accepted candidates to not enroll after all, according to survey findings released in October.

Those cuts were preceded by an anti-DEI directive that has since been heavily litigated and was most recently blocked in court in September.

That anti-DEI letter specifically called for agency personnel to review all new grant awards and issued grants to ensure those federal dollars “do not fund discriminatory practices — including in the form of DEI.” The directive added that “Illegal DEI policies and practices can violate both the letter and purpose of Federal civil rights law and conflict with the Department’s policy of prioritizing merit, fairness, and excellence in education.”

The Justice Department in August 2025 also warned districts they could be exposed to legal liability by asking job applicants how their “cultural background informs their teaching,” using recruitment strategies targeting candidates from specific geographic areas or racial backgrounds, and asking job candidates to describe how they overcame obstacles.

Since the Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, civil rights groups have raised concerns that it would set back educational equity efforts even outside of race-conscious admissions. That decision undid race-conscious policies in college admissions, and the Education Department under Trump has used it to justify scaling back other diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in education.

title: ‘The abuse I copped was phenomenal’: researchers accuse tobacco companies of intimidation tactics to silence critics
summary:
Exclusive: Industry tactics are part of ‘deliberate strategy’ to distort evidence and weaken regulation, paper says

full_text:
Prof Charlotta Pisinger, a medical doctor and public health researcher, was speaking to this journalist about her experiences of intimidation by the tobacco industry when another complaint to her employer landed in her inbox.

The Danish subsidiary of the tobacco company Philip Morris International (PMI) had just filed a complaint accusing her of breaching the University of Southern Denmark’s research communication standards for media interviews she gave questioning the safety of heated tobacco and vapes and whether PMI really cared about improving health.

“In countries where proper tobacco legislation is still not in place, they [the tobacco industry] still charge ahead and do everything they can to promote cigarettes,” she said in one interview.

The complaint from PMI stated: “Pisinger claims that PMI lies and deceives. We assume that Pisinger’s statements are to be understood polemically and not as an expression of a factual legal matter.”

The company also accused her of failing to clarify whether her comments reflected her scientific expertise or personal opinion, and accused her of overstating conclusions and omitting context in her media appearances.

A report published in the international journal Tobacco Control on Thursday and led by the Australian physician and epidemiologist Prof Emily Banks describes complaints to employers of tobacco control advocates as “not isolated incidents but part of a systemic challenge”.

The paper accuses the tobacco industry of using threats and complaints to employers as a tactic to push back against advocates, researchers and policymakers, describing this as “a deliberate strategy to silence critics, distort evidence, and weaken regulation”.

While it is not possible to establish tobacco industry involvement with certainty in all cases of intimidation, the paper says working in tobacco control nonetheless exposes researchers to a range of intimidation tactics, and calls on governments and employers to treat intimidation as an occupational health and safety issue.

Other tactics mentioned in the paper include public and online discreditation, including tobacco researchers being labelled as “zealots” and “extremists” while their work is misrepresented; being the target of freedom of information requests; and legal threats. The paper also offers practical strategies that people can use to anticipate, withstand and learn from pushback.

Banks says she has felt intimidated when she was abused online or when people have contacted her boss “and that person’s boss up the line to question the way I’m working”.

“Of course people have the right to seek information, but our paper finds that freedom of information requests can be weaponised for industry intimidation.”

Clandestine tactics

The paper accuses the tobacco industry of using clandestine tactics, operating through front groups and third parties, or using individuals and organisations whose affiliations are deliberately obscured. Otherwise legitimate actions are used in ways that disproportionately burden, discredit or deter those targeted, the paper argues.

The Australian National University associate professor Raglan Maddox, a co-author of the paper, says “the most abuse I have ever received in one day” came after he spoke publicly about the health of children being a human right during an inquiry into vaping. Many major vape brands are owned or supported by tobacco companies.

“I spoke about children grappling with nicotine addiction and not being able to sleep without having a vape under their pillow and the types of things we need to support them through nicotine addiction,” he says.

“The abuse I copped for 24 hours after that was phenomenal. Why would [the abusers] be questioning the way I look, my character, instead of an industry that continues to fuel 66 deaths a day in Australia, and 37% of all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander deaths?”

Maddox called out the Australian parliamentary inquiry into illicit tobacco, where public health experts testified publicly, while tobacco industry figures were permitted to give evidence behind closed doors and remain anonymous.

“While they stood in the same hallways as us, the public accountability … is very different,” Maddox says. “They’re protected from that scrutiny, and health practitioners don’t have that same privilege.”

While many researchers report contending with reputational, legal and bureaucratic attacks, the paper claims that in countries where advocates have little institutional or government backing, pushback has escalated to physical violence. Others have faced death threats, the paper alleges, although that remains rare.

‘Time-consuming and unpleasant’ to respond

The paper describes the toll that responding to and preventing intimidation takes on workers.

Pisinger, who says a tobacco company demanded she be fired from the hospital she worked at in 2013, says “every time” her employer receives a complaint, “I have to explain myself, provide documentation, and so on”.

“It is time-consuming and unpleasant until it is resolved.”

When questioned about Pisinger’s claims, a manager of corporate affairs for PMI in Denmark said the company “respects the right of academics to express their views, including views critical of our company”.

“Equally, we believe that claims presented as scientific fact should be open to scrutiny and challenge. Our complaint … does not seek to restrict [Pisinger’s] freedom to speak or participate in public debate.”

Lotus Sofie Bast, from the National Institute of Public Health in Denmark, researches tobacco and nicotine prevention among adolescents, and says she is concerned by the tobacco industry’s impact on young researchers in particular, who may be deterred from working in the field.

She was not involved in the study but says she and her legal department “spend hours” responding to freedom of information requests from the industry, and that representatives have also shown up at student PhD defences taking notes and wearing sunglasses inside.

At an event to launch data about youth nicotine use, the tobacco industry fought with her institute to be allowed to attend. In the end, Bast counted about 15 tobacco, nicotine and e-cigarette industry representatives in the room.

“There was kind of an odd feeling in the room, and comments from other participants were rather sparse,” she says.

The World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control requires governments to protect health policies from being influenced by the tobacco industry, a principle researchers including Pisinger and Bast also adhere to.

The paper calls on employers to support staff through complaints, and on governments to more strictly enforce rules barring tobacco industry interference in health policy.

The paper also outlines protective strategies for those working in the field, such as having a risk management plan, strengthening digital security, and documenting and reporting all threats.

“For those in tobacco control, the legacy will not be the attacks they endured, but the collective progress they helped secure,” the paper says.

title: How schools can help students shape their futures
summary:
Helping students develop their skills and navigate future career pathways is a key challenge for schools and counsellors. But what happens when it's not immediately clear where those skills could lead? The platform Knoo aims to help answer that question.

The post How schools can help students shape their futures appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
A student says he wants to work in technology because he likes solving problems. At his next meeting with his school counsellor, he mentions that his favourite part of a recent project was showing his classmates how to use what he had built. That detail changes the conversation.

The challenge for schools is to help students use discoveries like this, made at different points in their education, to decide what to explore and develop next.

In its analysis of PISA 2022, the OECD found that, on average across its member countries, 39% of 15-year-olds were unclear about their career expectations. It is reasonable to have doubts and change your mind at 15. The question for schools is how to use that period of uncertainty to give students time to try different paths, build skills and reconsider their choices in light of what they learn.

School counsellors pick up clues about a student through individual conversations, teachers’ observations, projects and experiences outside the classroom.

Even when those clues are available, turning them into a plan takes work. Which strengths does the student already draw on? What skill could they develop now? Where could they practise it, and what could they bring back to the next meeting to discuss?

School counsellors pick up clues about a student through individual conversations, teachers’ observations, projects and experiences outside the classroom

We created Knoo to support that work. It gives schools and counsellors a method and a platform for helping students understand their strengths and plan their development. Students begin with a questionnaire that generates a Human Potential Map. The counsellor and student interpret the map together, connect the responses to the student’s experiences and agree on a plan.

The platform brings the map, the plan and suggested learning activities together so they can revisit what they agreed and adjust the next step.

Take the student who enjoyed teaching his classmates. His counsellor might suggest that he lead a short workshop. He would have to prepare the session, explain an idea clearly and adapt his approach to the group’s questions. Afterwards, they could talk about what he enjoyed and what he found difficult. Does he want to spend more time building things, helping others use them or doing a bit of both? That experience gives him something concrete to draw on as he explores different roles and chooses what to practise next.

We use the Portuguese term Lugar de Potência for the place a student begins to find through this process. It describes the kinds of situations in which they can use their strengths in ways that matter to them and keep developing. Their understanding of that place can change as they try new roles. A school project, mentoring, an internship or a course can each give them a chance to learn something about themselves.

International education can offer one such opportunity. If a student wants to learn to collaborate across cultures, for example, an education agent can help the family compare programmes by looking at how students from different countries work together and what support they receive. The agent can use the student’s goal to make that comparison more specific. The school counsellor can help the student prepare for the experience and reflect on it afterwards.

A good guidance conversation gives a student something they can try. At the next meeting, they come back with an experience to make sense of, a skill to keep practising and a better basis for deciding what they want to do next.

title: Constraints on innovation in public higher education
summary: by David J. Finch, Chad Saunders, Stephen Murgatroyd, Nadège Levallet, Norm O’Reilly, & Hussein Al-Zyoud Governments have spent decades trying to make higher education more responsive. Performance-based funding, micro-credentials, work-integrated learning, and online delivery have all promised transformation. Yet institutions … Continue reading →
full_text:
by David J. Finch, Chad Saunders, Stephen Murgatroyd, Nadège Levallet, Norm O’Reilly, & Hussein Al-Zyoud

Governments have spent decades trying to make higher education more responsive. Performance-based funding, micro-credentials, work-integrated learning, and online delivery have all promised transformation. Yet institutions and credential structures have largely absorbed each of them.

The usual explanations point to rigid governance, cautious leadership, and conservative institutional cultures. These matter, but they cannot account for a pattern that repeats across systems and reform cycles.

In a forthcoming paper in Policy Reviews in Higher Education, we argue that the core question is not why institutions resist change, but why the system is structured to absorb it.

The bottleneck isn’t teaching. It’s recognition.

Our analysis draws on natural monopoly and contestability theory from the economics of regulated infrastructure. The claim isn’t that universities are monopoly firms, but that the focus should be on the shared infrastructure underpinning higher education and on who controls access to it.

That infrastructure has three functions:

Validation: the authority to formally recognise learning and award credentials.

Coordination: the rules that make credits and credentials portable across institutions and sectors.

Signalling: the processes through which credentials become trusted indicators of capability in the labour market.

Learning happens in many settings, including bootcamps, employer academies, and online platforms. Without access to trusted recognition, however, these pathways lack the portability and credibility of established credentials, and alternative pathways struggle to scale.

The problem is most acute in publicly dependent systems, where most students attend publicly subsidised institutions and public authorities control much of recognition and quality assurance. Canada, the UK, the Nordic countries, and much of continental Europe fit this model.

Where the rigidity comes from

Five structural conditions hold the system in place:

Concentrated validation infrastructure. Shared standards make credentials trustworthy, but authorised institutions and bodies control access to accreditation, assessment, and recognition, often favouring established models.

Inelastic credential demand. Enrolment is less price-sensitive than expected, because learners need recognised credentials, not just access to learning.

Vertical integration. Institutions typically design curricula, deliver instruction, assess learning, and award credentials, controlling the entire chain.

Reputational asymmetry. Employers use institutional prestige to reduce hiring uncertainty. Rankings and funding reinforce established hierarchies.

Concentrated signalling authority. Degrees remain the dominant hiring signal, even where they only partly reflect job-relevant capabilities.

The result is high barriers to entry, fragmented learning pathways, and innovations that are absorbed rather than scaled.

The consequences extend beyond universities. Adult and non-traditional learners struggle to have their learning recognised. Employers build their own assessments. Valuable learning from work, communities, and online platforms goes under-recognised.

In Canada, 21.8 per cent of core-aged workers with a postsecondary credential reported being overqualified for their job in 2025. Overqualification has many causes, but it raises questions about how well education translates into recognised labour-market value.

Lessons from other sectors

Telecommunications, utilities, rail, and banking have faced similar challenges. Their responses, including number portability, open banking, and separating infrastructure from service delivery, changed who could access essential systems.

The principle is clear: innovation depends not only on who provides a service, but also on who controls the infrastructure needed to participate.

For higher education, this suggests three policy interventions:

Power redistribution: shifting resources and choice toward learners through portable entitlements, learner-directed funding, and transparent recognition rules.

System unbundling: separating instruction from assessment and credential validation, so learning from different sources can earn comparable recognition.

Ecosystem governance: establishing independent stewardship of credential registries, interoperability standards, and trusted signalling infrastructure.

Each carries risks. Choice without support can reinforce inequality. Unbundling without standards can fragment the system. Independent regulators can be captured.

We therefore propose governed contestability, in which open access to shared infrastructure, inclusive quality standards, independent public stewardship, and equity safeguards work together.

This is not an argument for privatisation or deregulation. It is about preserving public trust while allowing diverse learning pathways to earn recognition.

Case studies and policy lessons

Three policy cases illustrate these principles.

Across the European Higher Education Area, the Bologna Process and related recognition initiatives established common standards to reduce barriers to cross-border mobility. Implementation remains uneven, but the case shows that shared coordination infrastructure can improve portability without altering institutional missions.

New Zealand’s Qualifications Authority established a national micro-credential framework that lets universities, private trainers, and industry organisations gain formal recognition under shared quality standards. This illustrates partial unbundling supported by independent stewardship, though long-term employer acceptance remains uncertain.

England provides a contrast. Following the Browne Review, reforms expanded student choice and opened funding to alternative providers, but institutional control over degree recognition and signalling remained largely intact. Competition increased within the existing hierarchy rather than changing it.

These cases are illustrative rather than causal tests, but they point to a common lesson: expanding choice without reforming control over validation and signalling risks reproducing the existing system.

Policy implications

Governments favour pilots, micro-credentials, and performance funding partly because these can be introduced without redistributing authority, which may also explain their limited system-level impact.

The paper sets out five diagnostic expectations, with measurable indicators, for distinguishing structural reform from institutional adaptation. Three questions capture their spirit: Are learners losing credits when transferring? Can alternative providers obtain recognition? Do employers trust alternative credentials?

The answers reveal whether reform changes the system’s architecture or adds programmes within it.

Universities do far more than award credentials. They advance research, preserve knowledge, and strengthen communities. This argument does not diminish those contributions; it separates their public value from their cManuscriptontrol over the infrastructure that recognises learning.

The aim is not to weaken universities, but to ensure that high-quality learning is recognised wherever and however it occurs, while protecting trust and equity.

For higher education reform to succeed, policy must tackle the bottleneck in recognition infrastructure rather than expect institutions to innovate around it.

David J. Finch is Professor of Innovation and Marketing at Mount Royal University and Visiting Fellow at Henley Business School. His research examines education, labour markets, human capital, and the relationship between learning, workforce development, and productivity.

Chad Saunders is a Professor at the University of Calgary’s Haskayne School of Business. His research examines entrepreneurship, innovation, organisational change, and higher education governance, with particular emphasis on the institutional conditions that shape adaptation and transformation.

Stephen Murgatroyd teaches anticipatory studies at the University of Alberta and Athabasca University. He has authored more than 40 books and delivers keynote presentations internationally on artificial intelligence, education, organisational transformation, and the future of work.

Nadège Levallet is an Associate Professor at the University of Maine and holds a PhD in Management Information Systems from Queen’s University. Her research examines digital technologies and organisational discontinuity, including their implications for institutional adaptation, human capital, and productivity.
